items.passage: Tromso in June never gets dark, and the wedding hall had its curtains open to a sky that refused to end the evening. I had come with an envelope in my jacket: the eight thousand kroner my aunt Wilhelmina had lent me eleven years earlier, when I was nineteen and stranded in Bergen without a ticket home. I found her near the cake table and pressed it into her hand. She looked at the envelope, thanked me for being so generous to the bride, and dropped it into the white box of cards by the door before I could explain. I stood there with my mouth open. Her old wristwatch, I noticed, had stopped at twenty past four, and she did not wind it all night. Hours later, during the speeches, the bride read aloud a card that had been tucked into my envelope, a card I had not written, thanking Devon and Wilhelmina together for their gift. Across the room my aunt raised her glass toward me and turned back to her conversation.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A nephew's attempt to repay an old loan goes awry at a crowded wedding.
A card read aloud reveals that an apparent mix-up was a way of declining repayment.
A shared card at a wedding shows that the aunt and nephew have grown close.
An aunt's confusion at the wedding leads her to write a card in both names.

items.passage: Brine and wet stone: that was the smell of the salt-water pool beside the Rhone on the Sunday mornings when Margaux's grandfather took her there. Ahanu swam badly and talked well. Between lengths he taught her words from the language of his childhood, across the ocean: the word for cold water, the word for a river that bends, the word for someone who is late coming home. She repeated them to the tiles and forgot most of them by Tuesday. He would not say who had taught him to swim. In March, fetching his coat from the hook, she found a folded letter addressed to a woman whose name she did not know, written in that language, unsent and creased many times along the same lines. She could read three words of it: cold water, a river that bends, someone late coming home. The following Sunday she arrived at the pool before him, and she was already reciting to the tiles when he came through the door.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A grandfather's swimming trips become an occasion for teaching his granddaughter words.
A granddaughter discovers an unsent letter her grandfather wrote to an unknown woman.
An unsent letter reveals the weight behind casual lessons, changing how she treats them.
Her eagerness to learn the language leads her grandfather to write an unsent letter.

items.passage: I was eleven when I carried the rumor home. Everyone in the school music room said that Siti, who had taught there since before I was born, was being sent away at the end of term, and I repeated it at dinner because it sounded important. My grandfather put down his spoon. He and Siti had not spoken in twenty years, for reasons no one at our table would name, and the next morning he put on his good shirt and walked to the school. I never learned what he said in the headmaster's office. The upright piano in the music room was locked that week, and its key hung on a nail no one would touch. By the cool season the story had come to nothing; Siti was staying. On Saturdays she began coming to our house with a satchel of sheet music, and from the kitchen I could hear two old players arguing over tempo, then starting the same bar again.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A boy repeats a rumor at dinner and prompts his grandfather to visit the school.
Two old musicians resume playing together at home after many years without speaking.
A grandfather's old quarrel with a teacher causes a rumor about her to spread.
A careless rumor carried home becomes the unexpected route to an old reconciliation.

items.passage: Reid came into the laundry house on Thursdays with his violin case under one arm and a bundle of shirts under the other. The steam, he said, kept his strings from going brittle in a Vermont January, and he would tune in the corner while the kettles boiled. I had taught him for six years, and I knew the habit; he tuned twice before every lesson as well. In November the letter had come from the Boston orchestra, a week after the audition date, and I had been the one who left it sealed in my coat pocket. Reid did not mention Boston to me. His first Thursday at the laundry was the week after that date had passed, and on that day he arrived before I did and took the tub beside mine. Each week since, he plays the audition piece once through while my shirts dry on the line. Last Thursday he took down the last of them, folded it collar first, and set it in my basket.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Reid most likely come to the laundry on Thursdays?
options: To protect his violin strings from the dry winter air while his laundry is washed.
To assure his teacher, without words, that he does not hold the delay against him.
To keep practicing the audition piece in case the orchestra offers him another date.
To remind his teacher, without words, of the audition that the letter cost him.

items.passage: Three rules governed the wall between Kwesi's beekeeper's yard and Kwame's house: no climbing, no smoke on windy days, and no talk of the photograph. Kwame kept the picture in a frame on his side, a print of two boys on one bicycle in front of the old hives, and he hung it in his window every morning facing the yard. Kwesi said he had moved his hives to the far corner years ago because the bees disliked the afternoon heat by the wall. For a long time he worked that corner with his back to the window. In the dry season of 1987, Kwame's son told the street that his father's eyes were failing, and that same week Kwesi began moving the hives, one each evening after dark, toward the wall again. He said nothing to Kwame about it. By March the last hive stood under the window, humming, and each morning Kwesi set a jar of the first honey on top of the wall, its label turned toward the house.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Kwesi most likely move the hives back toward the wall?
options: To give the bees a better place to forage now that the dry season has arrived.
To reclaim the part of the yard he had given up during their years of distance.
To bring the scene in the picture within reach of a neighbor losing his sight.
To apologize for the years he spent working with his back to the window.

items.passage: Leopoldina ran the boarding-house kitchen in Porto Alegre by the clock, and she ran me by it too: coffee at five, beans soaking by six, no salt in the pot until she had tasted it herself. When my mother's letter came saying there was work for me with a cousin in Montevideo, my aunt told me I could not possibly go before the feast of Sao Joao, since the house was full and she needed hands. I believed her. The boarders, after all, ate like regiments. But the letter, I saw later, was dated in April, and she gave it to me in June, on the morning after the feast. That week she stopped tasting the pot before I salted it. She let me order from the butcher alone. The night before the ship, she wrapped her own knife, the one with the cracked handle, in a dish towel and laid it at the bottom of my trunk.

To keep him from leaving before he could manage a whole kitchen by himself.
To shield him from a cousin's household that she considered unreliable.
To hold on to his company a little longer before letting him go abroad.

items.passage: Thessaloniki was still dark when Despina and I let ourselves into her uncle's bakery to practice, as we had every morning that winter, among the cooling racks. Flour on the music stand. Flour on the bow. Her uncle charged us nothing but the sweeping. The letter from the conservatory in Vienna lay folded inside her violin case, offering one place, for one player, beginning in March. We played the second movement and stopped at the bar where we always stopped. She tuned her A string. I tuned mine. Neither of us said Vienna. Outside, the first cart came for the bread. When we finished, I swept as usual, from the ovens to the door, and then I went back and swept the corner beneath her chair a second time, where there was nothing left to sweep, and set her case by the door with the clasp already fastened.

items.passage: "Hold the lamp lower," Kofi said, and Yaa did. She had come to his noodle stall near the Marina with his old school bell in a paper bag, the brass one he had rung for thirty years before the mission school closed, its clapper snapped off at the hinge. She had found a smith in Ebute Metta who would weld it for two shillings. Kofi turned the bell over in his hands between bowls. He tapped the weld with a chopstick. It gave a flat sound, a clack rather than a ring, and a customer at the bench laughed. Kofi laughed too, and ladled the man more broth. He told Yaa the smith had done good work, that the price was fair, and asked after her mother. When she rose to go, he wiped the bell with his apron, front and back, and set it on the shelf above the pot, mouth down, where the steam could reach it every morning.

items.passage: Four films a week in the season, one in the off-season: that was the rule at the Empire on Frederick Street, and in August even the one played to empty rows. Cecile ran the projector and called the owner Mr. Tomoe, as she had since she was twelve, and he called her Miss Cecile and paid her on Fridays from a tin box. The old doorman who had sold tickets there for forty years lay sick in the back room, asking every evening how the house had been. Tomoe told him full. Cecile said the man deserved to hear the truth. They argued about it on the stairs, politely, and Tomoe had the last word, as owners do. On Friday he opened the tin box and found it heavier than he had left it; the week's takings had been nine shillings, and there were thirty inside. He counted it twice and said nothing. That evening Cecile went into the back room first and told the doorman the house had been full.

Formally his employee, she relies on his generosity to keep her place at the theater.
Formally his employee, she covers his losses in secret and yields to his wishes.

items.passage: "Sit if you're staying, Master Ronan," Fergus said, and went on chalking the coat on his table. He had called me that since my father sailed for Boston, as if I were a customer and not a boy who had sat in his back room every evening for three months waiting for the post. I sat on the bolt of grey serge. He did not offer tea; he never did. At six the post boy came with nothing for us, and Fergus marked it in the ledger by the door, in the column he kept for my father's letters, a column of short dashes. When my boots split in October, a new pair appeared under the serge with no bill attached. I asked him what I owed. He said the account was settled and named no one who had settled it. On the last night before the news came, I fell asleep on the bolt and woke to find the lamp still lit and Fergus sitting up at the table with no coat in front of him.

When the conductor's steps came down the corridor, he set the compass on the seat between us, open, and kept his eyes on the glass; the conductor glanced at the cap and moved on. items.passage: Lakeside, my thirtieth summer, kept its promenade swept for visitors who were not us. Two herrings on Mondays, a smoked eel on Thursdays, and no credit: those were the terms Herr Gyeongho set when Katharina first came to his stall at the edge of the omnibus depot in Hamburg. She called him Herr Gyeongho, and he called her Fraulein, and they bargained each week over a pfennig as if the stall depended on it. In the winter her mother's wages from the depot laundry stopped. Katharina still came on Mondays and Thursdays and paid what she could, and he wrapped the fish without counting the coins. One afternoon, sent to fetch paper from under his counter, she opened the wrong drawer and found a ledger in her own family's name, page after page of small debts, every line crossed through in the same blue pencil. She closed the drawer. The next Monday she brought him a pfennig more than the price and set it on the scale before he could speak; he looked at it a long moment and let it lie there.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Katharina and Gyeongho?
A) Behind their formal bargaining lies a plain trade between a merchant and a regular buyer.
B) Behind their formal bargaining lies a protective generosity he extends to her family unseen.
C) Behind their formal bargaining lies a shared pleasure in haggling that both look forward to.
D) Behind their formal bargaining lies his reliance on her custom to keep the stall afloat.

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
앞부분의 'Herr', 'Fraulein'이라는 호칭과 외상 불가 규칙, 매주의 흥정은 공식적인 상거래 관계를 보여 준다. 그러나 중간에 그는 돈을 세지 않고 생선을 싸 주고, 서랍 속 장부에는 그녀 가족의 빚이 모두 같은 연필로 지워져 있어 비용을 조용히 떠안은 쪽이 그임이 드러난다. 끝에서 그는 그녀가 더 얹은 동전을 말없이 받아 들여 그녀의 체면을 지켜 준다. 따라서 그가 그녀 가족을 보이지 않게 돕는 관계를 말한 B가 정답이다. A는 호칭과 규칙만, C는 흥정 장면만 반영했고, D는 의존의 방향을 뒤집는다.
### lit40-hard-03-039 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism
[지문]
Hokkaido in February looked, from the overnight train, like a page no one had written on yet. I had no ticket. I had climbed into the last compartment at Sapporo because its blind was down, and the old man inside, whose cap still said CAPTAIN in faded thread, moved his feet to make room and went on looking out the window. For three hours neither of us spoke. At each station he took a brass compass from his coat, opened it, checked our heading against the timetable on his knee, and snapped it shut. When the conductor's steps came down the corridor, he set the compass on the seat between us, open, and kept his eyes on the glass; the conductor glanced at the cap and moved on. Near Asahikawa he spoke at last, to ask where I was going. I told him I did not know. He held out the compass, still open, closed my fingers around it, and lay back with his cap over his eyes.

[질문] In the passage, the compass most likely represents
A) a navigational tool he uses to confirm the train's progress at each stop.
B) the order and routine of his former life at sea, which he still keeps up.
C) a sense of purpose he hands on to someone who has not yet found one.
D) the trust between the two travelers, which his long silence had withheld.

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
처음에 나침반은 노인이 역마다 열차의 방향을 확인하는 도구로 등장한다. 중간에 차장이 다가오자 그는 나침반을 열어 두 사람 사이 좌석에 놓아 화자를 감싸는 데 쓰고, 끝에서는 갈 곳을 모른다는 화자의 손에 열린 나침반을 쥐여 주는 동작으로 바뀐다. 따라서 두 맥락을 모두 포괄해, 방향을 잃은 사람에게 넘겨주는 삶의 방향 감각을 뜻하는 C가 정답이다. A는 문자적 기능, B는 앞 맥락만 반영했고, D는 침묵을 관계의 단절로 보아 나침반을 건네는 마지막 동작의 의미를 관계 회복으로 잘못 읽는다.
### lit40-hard-03-041 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism
[지문]
Lakeside, my thirtieth summer, kept its promenade swept for visitors who were not us. Each evening I carried Mother's folding stool along the boards, opened it at the rail, and stood behind her while she watched the lake for the Buffalo steamer that had once brought my brother Cyrus home. Cyrus had gone east to read law on the money Father left; I had stayed, and the stool had come with staying. I learned to open it one-handed. In August a letter came saying that Cyrus would not visit that year either. Mother read it twice, folded it into her sleeve, and asked for nothing. That evening I set the stool down as usual, but my hand stayed a long while on the canvas seat, pressing where it sagged. At the end of the boards, when Mother rose to walk the last stretch on her cane, I did not fold it. I sat down upon it and watched the water myself, and she, after a moment, came back and stood beside me.

[질문] Based on the text, the folding stool most likely represents
A) a claim to ease the speaker has long yielded to others
B) the bodily frailty that makes the mother lean on her daughter
C) the mother's patient hope that Cyrus will someday come home
D) a distance between mother and daughter that the evening begins closing

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
의자는 처음에 화자가 어머니를 위해 펴 주는 도구로 등장하며, 오빠 Cyrus가 떠난 대가로 화자가 '남은 것'과 함께 주어진 짐이다. 편지 이후 화자는 의자 천을 오래 눌러 보며 그것을 대하는 태도가 달라지고, 마지막에 처음으로 직접 앉는다. 따라서 의자는 화자가 오랫동안 남에게 양보해 온 쉼과 돌봄받을 몫을 상징하므로 A가 정답이다. B는 의자의 문자적 기능, C는 앞 맥락(증기선을 기다림)만 반영하며, D는 마지막 장면을 관계 회복으로 읽었지만 결정적 동작은 화자 자신이 앉는 것이다.
### lit40-hard-03-042 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Irena had rented the farmhouse outside Gdansk because its old barn carried sound well and because the ensemble could not afford the city hall that season. Tatiana, the youngest violinist, had joined at fifteen; she was nineteen now, and a quartet in Berlin had written to her twice. All week she arrived early, unpacked her violin, and left the case open on the chair beside her, its velvet lining turned toward the door. Irena watched her play the slow movement with her shoulders lifted, a swallow perched on a wire that hums. On Friday the letter from Berlin lay on Tatiana's stand, still sealed, beneath the pencil she used to copy Irena's bowings into her part. During the break Irena said nothing about it. She only moved the chair with the open case a little closer to the stove, so that the lining would be warm whenever Tatiana chose to close it.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a swallow perched on a wire that hums” most nearly suggests that Tatiana is
A) poised to depart while still held by present ties
B) light and fragile in a way that weakens her playing
C) vibrating with a nervousness that unsettles the others
D) restless in a way common to young players generally

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
Tatiana에게는 베를린 4중주단의 편지가 두 번 왔고, 그녀는 매일 바이올린 케이스를 문 쪽으로 열어 둔다는 두 단서가 비유 앞에 있다. 비유 뒤에는 편지가 Irena의 보잉을 옮겨 적는 연필 아래 봉한 채 놓여 있다는 사소한 디테일이 나와, 떠날 준비만이 아니라 지금의 악단에 대한 애착도 함께 드러낸다. 따라서 '울리는 전선 위의 제비'는 떠날 채비를 하면서도 현재의 유대에 붙들린 상태를 뜻하므로 A가 정답이다. B는 가벼움, C는 소리·진동 속성만 골랐고, D는 의미를 젊은 연주자 일반으로 넓혔다.
### lit40-hard-03-043 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
I had not seen Ananya since the wedding where I knocked the garland tray from her hands in front of three hundred guests, and now our grandmother's funeral had placed us in the same borrowed classroom in Kochi, where the language school let the family receive visitors. Ananya sat at a front desk, straightening a stack of English primers no one would open that day. Each time an aunt came near, she squared the stack again and answered in short sentences. I took the desk behind her. Her silence toward me was a door left on the latch. When the tea came, she poured two cups and set one at the corner of her own desk, on the side nearest me, without turning around. Later, clearing the desks, I found Nikhil written small on the inside cover of the top primer, in the round hand she had used as a girl.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a door left on the latch” most nearly suggests that Ananya's silence is
A) a firm barrier meant to keep the narrator away
B) a guarded reserve that still allows the narrator in
C) a fragile calm that could give way under pressure
D) a general reluctance to talk with relatives today

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
화자는 결혼식에서 Ananya에게 망신을 준 과거가 있고, Ananya는 친척이 다가올 때마다 책 더미를 다시 정리하며 짧게만 대답한다는 두 단서가 비유 앞에 놓여 있다. 비유 뒤에는 그녀가 화자 쪽 책상 모서리에 찻잔을 놓는 사소한 행동이 나와, 침묵이 완전한 거부가 아님을 보여 준다. 따라서 '걸쇠만 걸린 문'은 경계하지만 다가갈 여지를 남긴 침묵을 뜻하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 차단의 속성만, C는 깨지기 쉬움의 속성만 골랐고, D는 의미를 친척 전반으로 넓혔다.
### lit40-hard-03-044 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Dariush counts the coins in his tin each evening
on the stone bridge, where the wind off the river
lifts the corners of Rukhsana's blue cloth.
The sum is not yet the sum he borrowed in spring.
She pins a hem against the railing, three fingers, then three,
and shows him again the blind stitch, the tailor's knot,
the way to bite a thread without fraying it.
Each night he opens the ledger to her page,
reads the figure written there, and closes it.
His debt to her is a lamp lit in a room he does not enter.
At noon the vendors cross with their baskets.
Her hands do not stop; neither do his.
When the light thins over the water
he takes the ledger out once more
and writes beneath the figure, not a payment,
only the day's date, in small careful letters,
the way she taught him to close a seam.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a lamp lit in a room he does not enter” most nearly suggests that Dariush's debt is
A) a warm gratitude that brightens his days on the bridge
B) a private shame that keeps him from speaking to her
C) an obligation he keeps tending while not settling it
D) a small expense he means to write down at some point

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
비유 앞에는 Dariush가 매일 저녁 동전을 세지만 빌린 액수에 이르지 못한다는 상황과, 매일 밤 장부의 그녀 페이지를 펴서 읽고 덮기만 하는 반복 행동이 놓여 있다. 비유 뒤에는 그가 금액이 아니라 날짜만 적어 넣는다는 디테일이 나와, 빚이 갚히지 않은 채 날마다 돌보아지고 있음을 보여 준다. 따라서 '들어가지 않는 방에 켜 둔 등불'은 갚지 못한 채 계속 돌보는 의무를 뜻하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 빛·따뜻함, B는 닫힌 방의 거리감 속성만 골랐고, D는 지문 표현(적기)을 문자적으로 읽은 해석이다.
### lit40-hard-03-045 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Steam and the smell of roasted barley tea met every traveler who stepped into Miriam's small cafe beside the Kyoto station. Shigeru came each afternoon for a month, ordered one cup, and rose when the four o'clock whistle sounded, though he boarded no train. At the door he bowed, then bowed again, then turned back to ask whether the cups were washed by hand or whether the rain would hold. Miriam, who had kept the cafe alone since her husband's death, answered each question and wiped a table that was already clean. His farewells were a kite string paid out slowly and not let go. One wet afternoon he left after a single bow. Miriam went to the window and stood there until the platform had emptied. The next day she set his cup on the counter before he arrived, its handle turned toward the door.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a kite string paid out slowly and not let go” most nearly suggests that Shigeru's farewells are
A) a playful habit meant to amuse the cafe's owner
B) a strained effort to leave a talk he dislikes
C) a general fondness for lingering in public places
D) a drawn-out parting that keeps the bond in place

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
비유 앞에는 Shigeru가 한 달 동안 기차를 타지도 않으면서 기적이 울리면 일어선다는 상황과, 문에서 두 번 절하고 다시 돌아와 질문하는 반복 행동이 놓여 있다. 비유 뒤에는 그가 단 한 번만 절하고 떠나자 Miriam이 창가에 서 있고 다음 날 그의 잔을 미리 내놓는 디테일이 나와, 길게 끄는 작별이 두 사람의 연결을 유지해 왔음을 보여 준다. 따라서 이 비유는 관계를 붙든 채 길게 늘이는 작별을 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 연의 놀이 속성, B는 줄의 팽팽함 속성만 골랐고, C는 의미를 공공장소 일반으로 넓혔다.
### lit40-hard-03-046 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Riga in the winter of 1912 left our courtyard fountain dry, its basin holding only leaves and the footprints of children. Frau Ingeborg owned the building; my aunt Zofia had rented the ground floor longer than I had been alive, and I had been sent to help her through the holidays. That year Ingeborg's Christmas Eve and Zofia's name-day fell on the same evening, and the courtyard had one table large enough for either. Each afternoon Zofia carried a chair out, set it beside the fountain, and sat facing the landlord's window with her shawl crossed tight. Her patience was a dry basin waiting for the thaw. On the evening itself Ingeborg came down with her own white cloth and laid it over half the table. Zofia smoothed her embroidered runner across the other half, and where the two fabrics met, she tucked her edge beneath Ingeborg's rather than over it.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a dry basin waiting for the thaw” most nearly suggests that Zofia's patience is
A) a readiness to receive held until the other acts
B) an emptiness left by years among strangers' rooms
C) a cold resentment stored against the landlord's house
D) a general weariness brought on by the long winter

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
비유 앞에는 두 전통의 명절이 같은 날 겹치고 식탁은 하나뿐이라는 상황과, Zofia가 매일 분수 옆에 앉아 집주인의 창을 바라보는 반복 행동이 놓여 있다. 비유 뒤에는 Zofia가 자신의 천 가장자리를 Ingeborg의 천 위가 아니라 아래로 넣는 사소한 디테일이 나와, 그녀의 기다림이 원한이 아니라 상대가 먼저 움직이면 받아들일 준비였음을 보여 준다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 빈 그릇의 공허, C는 겨울의 차가움 속성만 골랐고, D는 의미를 계절 일반의 피로로 넓혔다.
### lit40-hard-03-047 — skill words_in_context · 유형 word_in_context
[지문]
By the third week of July, Shira had stopped eating with the surveyors. I had come up from Tel Aviv to map the camp's new water line, and she farmed the fields beside it; each morning she carried her tray to the far end of the dining hall and ate facing the window, where the stakes I had planted the day before stood in her orchard. On Thursday the regional office approved my route without consulting her. Lior, the camp cook, set the approval letter beside her coffee. Shira read it and remained ______. She folded the letter into quarters, finished her bread, and then walked the length of the hall to my table and asked, in an even voice, to see the map.

[질문] Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) hot with anger
B) cool and composed
C) quiet and defeated
D) deep in planning

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
앞부분에서 Shira는 측량사들과 식사하지 않고 창가에서 말뚝을 바라보며 거리를 두는데, 이는 빈칸이 냉담함과 일관되어야 한다는 첫째 제약이다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그녀는 편지를 접고 빵을 다 먹은 뒤 차분한 목소리로 지도를 보여 달라고 하므로, 감정을 드러내지 않는 절제된 어조여야 한다는 둘째 제약이 생긴다. 두 제약을 모두 만족하는 것은 B다. A는 첫째 제약만 만족하고 차분한 목소리와 맞지 않으며, C는 정도가 지나쳐 직접 찾아가는 행동과 어긋나고, D는 지문의 계획·지도 소재를 빌렸을 뿐 뒤 행동과 맞지 않는다.
